title: Architecture Sinkhole / Pass-Through Layers
pattern: In a strictly layered architecture, an action or request traverses from the top layer to the bottom layer via simple pass-through calls, with no logical transformations or business rules applied at intermediate levels.
why_bad: It results in immense boilerplate and processing overhead, making changes extremely tedious. Adding a single field forces the developer to modify signatures and code across all adjacent layers, with zero architectural or encapsulation benefits.
detection: A series of nested functions/methods across physical directories or modules (e.g., `web` -> `domain` -> `db`) that perform identical delegate forwarding with matching signatures and no local logic.
counterexample: `Context-dependent`. Boundaries where strict security checks, RPC marshaling, or cross-network serialization are required.
fix: Adopt an "open" layered architecture style, allowing simple read/write requests to bypass intermediate layers when no business logic or transformation is required.
source: Mark Richards & Neal Ford, *Fundamentals of Software Architecture* (2020), Chapter 10 ("Layered Architecture Style - Architecture Sinkhole"), p. 138.
